title: The midget subs sail
pull: Ten men, five tiny boats, one secret target

facts.text: On 18 November 1941, five big Imperial Japanese Navy submarines, I-16, I-18, I-20, I-22 and I-24, left the naval base at Kure. Together they were the Special Attack Unit, and their target was Pearl Harbor.
The day before, the unit's officers were briefed on the Hawaii Operation at the Kure Naval Club.
From Kure the five boats went to the Kamegakubi Naval Proving Ground, where each took on a top secret two man Type A midget submarine. At 2:15 a.m. on 19 November they sailed for Hawaii.
Each midget rode on the mother submarine's deck behind the conning tower, held down by steel bands.
A Type A midget was 23.9 meters (78 feet 5 inches) long, displaced 46 tons, and carried two men and two torpedoes.
The plan was for the midgets to slip into Pearl Harbor, wait out the air raid, and fire their torpedoes, then meet their mother submarines again after dark on 7 December. None of the five came back.
One midget was sunk by the destroyer USS Ward at the harbor entrance early on 7 December, before the planes arrived.
I-24's midget, HA-19, was crewed by Ensign Kazuo Sakamaki and Petty Officer Kiyoshi Inagaki. Its gyrocompass did not work, and it spent the morning bumping along the reef outside the harbor.
Nine of the ten men died. Inagaki drowned; Sakamaki washed ashore on Oahu on 8 December and was taken by Corporal David Akui, becoming the first Japanese prisoner of war held by the United States.
At home the nine dead were hailed as war heroes, often called the nine war gods. Sakamaki's name was left out.

photoNote: Sakamaki's midget submarine HA-19 aground in the surf at Bellows Field (Waimanalo), Oahu, with lines run to the hull, December 1941. US Navy photo, NARA 80-G-32680 (naId 12009051), original caption describes a captured Japanese two man submarine at Bellows Field after the attack of 7 December 1941, use Unrestricted, US government work, public domain. Cropped slightly from the scan, 1920 x 1503, grayscale. Taken 8 December or soon after, not on the sailing date: it shows how the voyage ended. Frame on the conning tower; the headland at right reads well. Alternative closer view: NARA 80-G-17079 (vertical).
photoCredit: The Japanese midget submarine HA-19 aground off Bellows Field, Oahu, December 1941. US Navy photo, NARA 80-G-32680, public domain.

declassified.fact: Sakamaki spent the war in American prison camps. Afterward he joined Toyota, rose to run its subsidiary in Brazil from 1969, and died in Japan in 1999. His boat, HA-19, survived too: it is on display at the National Museum of the Pacific War in Fredericksburg, Texas.

body:
Each one rode to war on the deck of a bigger submarine, held down by steel bands.

18 November 1941. Five big submarines of the Imperial Japanese Navy, I-16, I-18, I-20, I-22 and I-24, left the naval base at Kure as the Special Attack Unit. Their target was Pearl Harbor. Each took on a top secret two man Type A midget submarine, 78 feet long with two torpedoes, and in the early hours of 19 November they sailed for Hawaii.

The plan was for the midgets to slip into the harbor, wait out the air raid, then fire. None of the five came back. Nine of the ten men died. The tenth, Ensign Kazuo Sakamaki, washed ashore on Oahu and became the first Japanese prisoner of war held by the United States.
